tldr: This study demonstrates that simply changing the twisted-yarn architecture—specifically how many conductive yarns are twisted together—allows flexible tuning of both pressure sensitivity and proximity detection range in textile capacitive sensors, enabling collision avoidance and touch control for robotic arms.
hero_caption: Schematic showing the twisted configurations of one, two, and four yarns (a) and the dramatic expansion of the effective electrode overlap area at the crossing points (b–e). Merely increasing the number of twisted yarns expands the electrode area by up to 16 times, clearly illustrating the substantial shifts in internal electric field and sensing performance.
overview:
To allow robots to collaborate safely with humans, robotic skins (electronic skins) must be capable of detecting both pre-contact "proximity" and post-contact "force (pressure)." Textile-based sensors are attracting significant attention because they conform naturally to curved surfaces and offer high breathability. However, previous work has focused predominantly on developing novel materials or fabric weave structures, leaving the specific impact of "yarn-level architecture" on sensing behavior largely unquantified.

To tackle this, the authors prepared conductive silver-coated yarns uniformly coated with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) insulation and twisted them into one-, two-, and four-layer configurations. Without changing any materials or manufacturing processes, they systematically explored how these purely geometric architectural differences dictate sensor performance.

Experiments revealed that increasing the yarn layer count expands the contact area at intersection points by up to 16 times, drastically boosting pressure sensitivity and tensile strength. At the same time, they identified a clear trade-off: a denser yarn architecture confines the surrounding fringing electric fields, thereby shortening the non-contact proximity detection distance. Finally, integrating this textile sensor onto a robotic arm enabled pre-contact autonomous avoidance, intuitive touch teleoperation, and context-aware emergency stops distinguishing human hands from metallic parts, all with an end-to-end system latency of approximately 403 ms.
contributions: Quantified for the first time how twisting conductive yarns into one-, two-, and four-layer configurations alters the effective electrode overlap area and inter-fiber separation in textile capacitive sensors.
Established design guidelines for tuning pressure sensitivity and proximity sensing range to specific applications purely through yarn geometric architecture, without altering chemical formulations.

Conducted rigorous stress evaluation based on localized single-fiber contact areas (around 0.07 mm²), demonstrating outstanding operational stability over 15,000 load cycles and across a temperature range of 25 to 90 °C.
Realized real-time spatial contact mapping with a 4×4 textile array, as well as collision avoidance, touch control, and material-discriminating safety stops on a Franka Emika Panda robotic arm.

sections.heading: Why Robotic Skin Needs Both Pre- and Post-Contact Sensing
sections.summary: Textile sensors are promising candidates for flexible electronic skins on curved robotic surfaces. Capacitive sensing is especially advantageous because it can capture proximity and pressure with a single device, but the impact of yarn-level twist architecture on its behavior remained unexplored.
sections.details:
When humans and robots share workspace, having soft, conformable robotic surfaces is essential for safety. Electronic textiles (smart fabrics) represent a prime candidate for achieving this. While sensing mechanisms range from piezoresistive to piezoelectric, capacitive transduction stands out due to its low power consumption, signal stability, and unique ability to capture both pre-contact proximity and post-contact pressure through the same operating principle.

Conventional textile capacitive sensors have mostly relied on sandwich structures that place a dielectric layer between two electrode sheets, or on planar interdigital electrodes. However, these designs face complex fabrication requirements and strong dependence on global fabric deformation. To address this, researchers introduced yarn-based approaches, in which insulated conductive yarns cross in a grid-like pattern, turning each yarn intersection into a microscopic sensing unit.

Nevertheless, prior studies have focused heavily on novel material synthesis or macroscopic weaving patterns. The influence of yarn-level geometric parameters—such as the number of twisted yarns—on effective electrode area, inter-fiber separation, pressure sensitivity, and proximity range remained unquantified. The authors had previously developed piezoresistive yarn sensors, but resistive sensors are susceptible to thermal drift and cannot detect proximity.

In this work, the authors introduce a textile capacitive sensing platform where pressure sensitivity and proximity detection range can be tailored at will simply by varying the twisted-yarn architecture (one, two, or four layers) without altering the constituent materials.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Fiber Sensors and the Missing Link in Yarn Architecture
sections.summary: While previous works have explored braided structures or helical liquid-metal fibers, none systematically investigated how multi-layer twisted-yarn architectures govern capacitive behavior and dual-mode proximity/pressure sensing within a unified platform.
sections.details:
Textile-integrated pressure sensors have advanced rapidly in recent years. Notable examples include highly sensitive braided structures utilizing ion-conducting yarns, helical liquid-metal yarn strain sensors engineered for high stretchability, and methods that tune performance by tailoring fiber diameter or porous microstructures.

Multimodal sensors capable of detecting both pre-contact proximity and post-contact pressure have also been developed for robotic skins. Examples include all-fabric tactile arrays as well as polymer-composite skins combining proximity, tactile, and thermal feedback.

However, existing literature presents two critical gaps:
- First, no prior work systematically and quantitatively investigated how multi-layer twisted-yarn architectures dictate effective electrode overlap area, inter-fiber separation, and capacitive response within a unified platform. Prior studies focused either on fabric-level weaves or single specialized fibers.
- Second, very few studies integrated such architected textile sensors into functioning robotic systems to validate practical capabilities like pre-touch collision avoidance and intuitive control.

This work fills these gaps by leveraging yarn twisting—a simple, scalable technique—to offer an alternative route to sensor tuning that does not rely on complex chemical synthesis.

sections.heading: From Continuous Nozzle Coating to Weaving: Engineering Twisted-Yarn Geometry
sections.summary: Silver-coated conductive yarns were continuously insulated with silicone rubber (PDMS) via nozzle coating and twisted into one-, two-, and four-layer configurations. These were stitched into a grid on a woven fabric substrate, turning each crossing point into a sensing element.
sections.details:
The fabrication workflow and measurement principles rely on clean, highly reproducible methods.

### Sensor Design and Scalable Fabrication
Commercial silver-coated yarns (diameter ~0.3 mm, linear resistance ~30 $\Omega/\mathrm{cm}$) served as the conductive core. These yarns combine excellent electrical conductivity with sufficient mechanical robustness for textile machinery. PDMS (polydimethylsiloxane) was chosen as the insulating dielectric coating. The yarns were continuously drawn through a nozzle filled with uncured PDMS at a line speed of 10 m/min, followed by thermal curing in an 80 °C heating chamber, forming a uniform insulation layer roughly 0.2 mm thick.

These coated yarns were then twisted into single-strand ("1-layer"), two-strand ("2-layer"), and four-strand ("4-layer") assemblies. Helical twisting prevents individual fibers from sliding relative to one another during mechanical loading, dramatically boosting structural integrity. Finally, these twisted yarns were stitched into a plain polyester woven fabric at a ~10 mm pitch along the warp and weft directions, creating a 30×30 mm² sensor sheet where each yarn crossover acts as an independent sensing node.

### Operating Principle and Stress Normalization
The capacitive response can be approximated by the parallel-plate capacitor equation, $C = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r A_{\mathrm{eff}} / d_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Under applied pressure, the PDMS coating at the intersection compresses, decreasing the effective inter-electrode distance $d_{\mathrm{eff}}$ while expanding the effective contact area $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$, which leads to an increase in capacitance $C$.

A key aspect of this study is how stress was determined. Rather than dividing the force by the gross sensor sheet area, the authors computed localized pressure using Hertzian contact mechanics for a single-fiber crossover area (~0.07 mm²), corresponding to stresses of 0.4 to 3.9 MPa. This provides a physically accurate stress representation linked to intrinsic material deformation.

### Characterization and Robotic Integration
Frequency characteristics were examined with an LCR meter at 1 kHz, 10 kHz, and 100 kHz. The sensors underwent thermal testing between 25 and 90 °C, tensile/compression testing, and a 15,000-cycle durability evaluation. Proximity sensing was tested against human hands, metals, and plastics. Finally, a 4×4 array was interfaced with a PSoC 6 microcontroller for real-time contact mapping and mounted onto a Franka Emika Panda robotic arm for system validation.

(b) Expansion of the effective electrode overlap area at crossing points from 0.25 to 1.0 and 4.0 mm² with increasing layer count. (c–e) Cross-sectional schematics illustrating how twisting increases contact area and reduces separation while progressively confining the outer fringing electric fields (yellow arrows).

sections.heading: Four-Layer Yarns Deliver Peak Sensitivity, but Reveal a Proximity Trade-Off
sections.summary: Thanks to a 16-fold expansion in electrode area, the four-layer sensor achieved the highest sensitivity (0.1331 MPa⁻¹) and superior mechanical strength. However, field confinement shortened its proximity range to 40 mm compared to 60 mm for the single-layer sensor.
sections.details:
Experimental evaluations confirmed that the twisted-yarn architecture dictates mechanical, electrical, and sensing behaviors alike.

### Pressure Response and Mechanical Toughness
Under step stresses between 0.4 and 3.9 MPa, all configurations showed stable, plateau-like responses that returned precisely to baseline upon release. The four-layer yarn exhibited the largest relative capacitance change ($\Delta C/C_0$) across the entire pressure range. In tensile tests, elongation at break rose from 37.5% (1-layer) to 62.5% (2-layer) and 85.0% (4-layer), while the maximum tensile load quadrupled from 23.3 N to 42.7 N and 89.7 N. Pressure sensitivity increased with test frequency, reaching its peak of $0.1331~\mathrm{MPa}^{-1}$ for the four-layer sensor at 100 kHz.

While step response and recovery times were around 0.9 s, the sensor tracked periodic dynamic oscillations from 1 to 5 Hz without waveform distortion or signal attenuation.

### Cyclic Durability and Hysteresis
Static loading with a 100 g weight showed virtually no signal drift, and cyclic testing over 15,000 cycles on a motorized stage demonstrated fatigue-free, stable performance. Loading and unloading cycles up to 1 kg exhibited negligible hysteresis, with forward and reverse curves nearly overlapping due to the elastic recovery of the PDMS dielectric.

### Thermal Stability and the Proximity Detection Trade-Off
Capacitance exhibited virtually zero systematic thermal drift between 25 and 90 °C, proving high environmental resilience without the need for active compensation circuits.

In proximity detection, approaching objects perturb the fringing fields, increasing capacitance. High-permittivity human hands and conductive metal plates elicited the strongest signals. Notably, the maximum proximity detection range decreased as the number of twisted strands increased: 60 mm for 1-layer, 50 mm for 2-layer, and 40 mm for 4-layer. Densely twisting yarns expands the contact area and enhances tactile pressure sensitivity, but simultaneously confines the external fringing field, revealing a fundamental architecture-dependent sensitivity-range trade-off.

### Robotic Arm Integration and Demonstration
Mounted on a Franka Emika Panda robot, the textile sensor performed three key tasks:
- Reflexive collision avoidance: retreating autonomously when a hand approached before contact occurred.
- Intuitive touch teleoperation (HMI): guiding the robot's motion based on direct touch inputs on the sensor surface.
- Context-aware safety stops: allowing normal gripper manipulation when handling metal gears, but triggering an immediate safety stop when an approaching human finger was detected.

The end-to-end system latency—from signal detection and processing to robot actuation—was approximately 403 ms, fast enough for real-time human-robot collaboration.

sections.heading: Tailoring Yarn Architecture: A New Blueprint for Soft Robotic Skins
sections.summary: This study showed that altering the twisted-yarn layer count alone can expand electrode overlap area by 16 times, providing versatile control over pressure sensitivity and proximity range. This geometric strategy, free from chemical reformulation, offers a powerful design guideline for soft robotics and wearables.
sections.details:
This work establishes that a single geometric parameter—the twisted architecture of PDMS-insulated conductive yarns—can be harnessed to tailor the full spectrum of capacitive sensing properties to target applications.

Transitioning from 1-layer to 4-layer yarns expanded the effective electrode overlap area from 0.25 mm² to 4.0 mm² (a 16-fold increase), simultaneously delivering elevated pressure sensitivity, heightened tensile strength, robust endurance over 15,000 cycles, and thermal stability from 25 to 90 °C. At the same time, quantifying the structural trade-off with proximity detection range (close-range tactile sensitivity versus long-range non-contact detection) provides a theoretical foundation for selecting the ideal layer count for a given application.

Because this method integrates seamlessly with standard textile manufacturing processes without requiring complex nanomaterial synthesis or microfabrication, it is exceptionally well-suited for scalable production. Moving forward, this geometric approach holds great promise for application across large-area collaborative robots, prosthetic limbs, and smart garments.

takeaways: Without changing chemical formulations, simply twisting conductive yarns into one, two, or four strands expands electrode overlap area by up to 16 times, broadly tuning sensor characteristics.

Increasing the layer count enhances tactile pressure sensitivity and tensile strength, but introduces a clear trade-off by confining fringing fields and shortening the proximity detection range (60 mm down to 40 mm).
Using PDMS insulation provides near-zero thermal drift from 25 to 90 °C and outstanding durability across 15,000 loading cycles.
A single textile sensing patch successfully executed proximity avoidance, touch control, and context-aware safety stops on a robotic arm with an end-to-end system latency of 403 ms.
limitations: The sensor exhibits a response and recovery time of approximately 0.9 s under step loading, which may be slow for capturing high-speed impact transients (though it reliably follows continuous periodic vibrations up to 5 Hz).

In proximity detection, capacitance shifts depend strongly on the target's dielectric constant and electrical conductivity, which can lead to distance estimation errors if target materials vary unpredictably.

Robotic arm tests were performed with sensors mounted on planar or gently curved surfaces; full conformability and signal stability under severe joint deformation or complex 3D compound curvatures remain to be validated.
